about: The new-app intake (ADR-0058): the question cards the new-app skill shows, and the test tools for each kind of test. New-KitApp checks the answers against this file and writes them to the app's docs/app-profile.md. Each card, and each role a kind of test fills, carries two labeled recommendations (ADR-0074): the authority's, only what its page says, with the page and the date read (pick null when the page names no pick, or the search that found no page; a pick only where the page recommends it, says it should be used, or gives it a guideline level such as CONSIDER, never where it only permits, uses or gives an example), and the agent's, with its reason. The developer's own preferences live in their preferences file, outside every repo (docs/preferences.md). A default is the developer's preference, then the authority's pick unless it's Paid (ARC-012), then the agent's. A card with dependsOn shows only the options whose fits lists the other card's answer, and has a recommendation for each answer that leaves more than one option. Every option and tool has a cost label: Free, Free tier (free up to a limit) or Paid, with the price, its source and the date checked, apart from all three recommendations.

cards.question: What kind of app is it?

authority.says: Names no app type. For a web UI it says: "For new project development, we recommend ASP.NET Core Blazor."

agent.reason: Fits most apps people use in a browser: the web UI is Blazor, which Microsoft recommends for a new web UI, and the API can serve a phone app later.

options.label: Web API and a Blazor web app
options.description: An ASP.NET Core API with a Blazor web front end. The API can serve a phone app later. Fits most apps people use in a browser.

options.label: Web API only
options.description: An ASP.NET Core HTTP API with no user interface of its own, for other apps or services to call.

options.label: Blazor web app only
options.description: A Blazor web app with no separate API: the pages read and write the data themselves.

options.label: .NET MAUI app (phone or desktop)
options.description: A native app for Android, iOS, Windows or macOS, built with .NET MAUI.

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: Its Windows and macOS builds cost nothing on a public repo, where GitHub Actions' standard runners are free; a private repo first spends its plan's included Actions minutes (ADR-0059)
cost.price: a private repo pays for each pull request's Windows and macOS builds by the minute: $0.010 a minute on Windows and $0.062 on macOS, against $0.006 on Linux

cards.question: Where does the app keep its data, and what shape is it?

authority.says: No recommendation: it matches each data store to the workload's goals and data model.

agent.reason: Most business apps have records that refer to each other, and the kit's rules and checks for migrations cover relational data (docs/database-guide.md).

options.label: On a server, as related tables
options.description: Records that refer to each other, such as customers and their orders, shared by every user. Most business apps.

options.label: On a server, as documents
options.description: Items read by one key, with a shape that changes often, or data spread across regions.

options.label: Only on the user's device
options.description: Each user's data stays in the app on their phone or computer; nothing is shared.

options.label: It keeps no data
options.description: The app stores nothing of its own, for example a calculator or a front end to another service.

authority.says: No pick between these two: it recommends SQL Database to build apps on a managed SQL database, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL for apps on PostgreSQL. It doesn't mention the free offer.

agent.reason: Free up to a monthly limit and paused rather than billed past it, with no end date, where PostgreSQL's free amount ends after 12 months; tests run on SQL Server in a container (docs/database-guide.md).

options.label: Azure SQL Database, free offer
options.description: SQL Server in Azure, free up to a monthly limit, and paused rather than billed past it. Tests run on SQL Server in a container.

options.label: Azure Database for PostgreSQL
options.description: PostgreSQL in Azure: free for 12 months with an Azure free account, then billed.

options.label: Azure Cosmos DB, free tier
options.description: A document database in Azure, free up to 1000 RU/s and 25 GB for the account's life.

options.label: SQLite
options.description: A database in a file inside the app. Free.

options.label: No database
options.description: The app keeps no data.

cards.question: Who signs in to the app?

authority.says: Picks by who signs in, not one for every app: an external tenant for apps for consumers and business customers, a workforce tenant for employees.

agent.reason: Kit apps are public by default (ADR-0033), so most are used by people outside one organization; it's free for the first 50,000 monthly active users.

options.label: Customers or the public
options.description: People sign in with Microsoft Entra External ID: email, or a Google or Microsoft account. The app never stores passwords (SEC-008).

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: The first 50,000 monthly active users; add-ons such as SMS codes have no free amount

options.label: People in one organization
options.description: Staff sign in with their work account in Microsoft Entra ID. The app never stores passwords (SEC-008).

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: Microsoft Entra ID Free: users, groups and single sign-on
cost.price: Microsoft Entra ID P1 and P2, for Conditional Access and ID Protection, not verified

options.label: No sign-in
options.description: Everyone sees the same thing and nobody signs in. Every endpoint is then public on purpose (SEC-017 applies to an app where most or all endpoints require sign-in).

authority.says: No recommendation without the workload: its flowchart picks a candidate service from the workload's needs.

agent.reason: Nothing to pay or set up until the first deployment is due, when the app's real needs can pick the service.

options.label: Not yet: on this machine and in CI
options.description: Build and test it first; choose hosting when the first deployment is due. Nothing to pay or set up now.

options.label: Azure Container Apps
options.description: Runs the app in a container that scales to zero when nobody uses it.

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: Each month, per subscription: 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds and 2 million requests
cost.price: Consumption plan, East US: $0.000024 per vCPU-second and $0.000003 per GiB-second while active, $0.40 per million requests

options.label: Azure App Service
options.description: Runs the app on a managed web server, without containers.

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: The F1 plan: shared compute with daily limits, no custom domain certificate and no scale-out (limits not verified)
cost.price: B1, the first paid plan, East US: $0.017 an hour on Linux, $0.075 an hour on Windows

cards.question: How much may this app cost each month?

authority.says: No amount: it asks for realistic budgets that cover the workload's functional and nonfunctional requirements.

agent.reason: Every kit default starts free, so a first app can cost nothing, and a budget can rise later through an ADR.

options.label: $0: free options only
options.description: Every tool and service starts on its free option. A paid one is still listed with its price, and spending needs your OK (ARC-012).

options.label: Up to $20 a month
options.description: Plans may pick a paid option when it fits better and its estimated price stays within $20 a month. Spending still needs your OK.

options.label: Up to $100 a month
options.description: Plans may pick paid options that fit better, within $100 a month in all. Spending still needs your OK.

testKinds.name: Unit
testKinds.checks: One class or function: domain rules, application handlers, view models

authority.says: No recommendation: it calls MSTest, NUnit, TUnit and xUnit.net the popular test frameworks.

agent.reason: Free (Apache-2.0), runs on Microsoft.Testing.Platform in v3, and is what the kit's sample and shared CI run.

authority.says: Calls Moq and NSubstitute popular mocking libraries for .NET, without a pick.

agent.reason: Free (BSD-3-Clause) for any app, so it never needs a paid license, and the kit's sample tests use it.

authority.says: No Microsoft Learn page found that names an assertion library; its pages show each test framework's own Assert.
authority.searched: fluent assertion library for .NET unit tests recommended

agent.reason: Free for any app (Apache-2.0), with FluentAssertions' API and namespace; FluentAssertions 8 needs a paid license once an app is sold (ADR-0004).

authority.says: No Microsoft Learn page found that names a fake-data library.
authority.searched: .NET tests generate fake test data library property-based testing mock HTTP server WireMock

agent.reason: Free (MIT); generates realistic test data from rules, so tests don't hand-write it.

authority.says: No Microsoft Learn page found that names a property-based testing library.
authority.searched: .NET tests generate fake test data library property-based testing mock HTTP server WireMock

agent.reason: Free (BSD-3-Clause); generates many inputs for one property, and runs from xUnit.

authority.says: No pick: it says "you can use FakeTimeProvider" to test time-dependent code, and names no other fake.

agent.reason: Microsoft's own fake for TimeProvider, free (MIT); TST-010 asks for time through a seam.

authority.says: No pick: it says FakeLogger "is intended for use in unit tests", capturing what's logged for the test to inspect.

agent.reason: Microsoft's own, free (MIT), and no mock of ILogger is needed.

tools.name: FluentAssertions 8

cost.label: Free tier
cost.free: Non-commercial use: free while the app isn't sold or paid for
cost.price: A commercial app needs an Xceed license, reported at $129.95 per developer a year at launch (not verified on xceed.com), or swaps to AwesomeAssertions, which is free (ADR-0004)

tools.note: Free for a non-commercial app only; a commercial one uses AwesomeAssertions instead (ADR-0004)

tools.name: AwesomeAssertions
tools.note: FluentAssertions' API and namespace under Apache-2.0, free for any app (ADR-0004)

testKinds.name: Integration
testKinds.checks: Our code plus one real outside thing: database, HTTP service, file system

authority.says: Recommends testing against the production database system, and names Testcontainers as one library that can help.

agent.reason: Free (MIT); starts the real engine in a container for each test run, as DAT-005 asks.

authority.says: No pick: to clear the database between tests it shows EF Core APIs and raw SQL, and says you "may also want to consider" the respawn package.

agent.reason: Free (Apache-2.0); clears test data without listing the tables.

authority.says: No Microsoft Learn page found that names a library for faking HTTP services.
authority.searched: .NET tests generate fake test data library property-based testing mock HTTP server WireMock

agent.reason: Free (Apache-2.0); a real HTTP server the test controls, so the app's HttpClient pipeline runs as in production.

testKinds.name: Functional
testKinds.checks: The whole app in a test host, through its real HTTP pipeline; Blazor components

authority.says: No pick among tools: its integration tests are built on WebApplicationFactory, from Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing, whose use "streamlines test creation and execution".

agent.reason: Microsoft's own, free (MIT); runs the app's real HTTP pipeline in the test.

authority.says: There's no official Microsoft testing framework for Blazor; it names bUnit, which Microsoft doesn't maintain, as an example library.

agent.reason: Free (MIT); the library Microsoft's Blazor testing page shows.

testKinds.name: UI (end to end)
testKinds.checks: The running system in a real browser, accessibility included
testKinds.runs: Every PR, in the shared .NET CI

authority.says: Names Playwright for .NET as an example of an end-to-end testing framework for Blazor apps.

agent.reason: Free (MIT), from Microsoft; drives real browsers in CI (ADR-0061).

authority.says: Its Power Platform Playwright samples audit pages with axe-core through a JavaScript package; no page found names a .NET package.

agent.reason: Free (MIT, with an MPL-2.0 engine); runs axe-core's WCAG checks from the .NET Playwright tests (ADR-0061).

authority.says: Its Blazor testing page names no way to host the app for end-to-end tests.

agent.reason: Free (MIT); hosts the app on Kestrel for the browser without an Aspire AppHost, as the kit's web UI fixture does (ADR-0061).

tools.name: Deque axe for Playwright
tools.note: Its axe-core engine, Deque.AxeCore.Commons, is MPL-2.0

tools.name: WebApplicationFactory on Kestrel
tools.note: Hosts the app on Kestrel for the browser (UseKestrel), for an app without an Aspire AppHost; as in the kit's web UI fixture (ADR-0061)

tools.name: Aspire testing
tools.note: For an app with an Aspire AppHost: starts the whole app for the browser

testKinds.name: System (smoke)
testKinds.checks: The deployed app in staging actually works

authority.says: Names Playwright for .NET as an example of an end-to-end testing framework for Blazor apps.

agent.reason: Free (MIT); the same tool as the UI tests, pointed at the deployed app.

testKinds.name: Architecture
testKinds.checks: Layers and modules depend only in allowed directions

authority.says: No Microsoft Learn page found that names a tool for checking dependency rules in tests.
authority.searched: architecture tests enforce layer dependencies .NET NetArchTest ArchUnitNET clean architecture

agent.reason: Free (Apache-2.0); checks layer and module dependencies as tests, with xUnit v3 support.

authority.says: No recommendation for a snapshot test; it notes a document generated at build time can be committed to source control or used for spec-based integration testing.

agent.reason: Free; fails a PR whose API document changed without the committed snapshot changing, as the kit's sample does.

authority.says: "CONSIDER enabling Package Validation" to detect breaking changes automatically.

agent.reason: Part of the .NET SDK, free; for apps that publish NuGet packages.

tools.name: OpenAPI snapshot test
tools.note: The API's OpenAPI document must match a committed snapshot, which the kit's shared OpenApiTests check in the FunctionalTests project, at Contract/<host name>/openapi-v1.json

tools.name: .NET package validation
tools.note: Part of the .NET SDK; for apps that publish NuGet packages

testKinds.name: Performance
testKinds.checks: Hot paths stay within their time and memory budget

authority.says: For benchmarking EF Core queries, "it's strongly recommended to use the well-known BenchmarkDotNet library".

agent.reason: Free (MIT); handles warm-up and iteration counts, which hand-written timings get wrong.

testKinds.name: Load
testKinds.checks: The app keeps its response times and error rate within budget under many users at once
testKinds.runs: Nightly or on demand, against the app started in CI; against a deployment once it has one

authority.says: Describes Azure Load Testing and lists third-party tools, Locust, Apache JMeter and NBomber among them, without a pick.

agent.reason: Free (MIT); runs in GitHub Actions at no cost on a public repo, and the kit's performance workflow already runs it against a budget (ADR-0062).

tools.name: Locust
tools.note: Runs in GitHub Actions: free on a public repo; a private one uses its account's Actions minutes (ADR-0057)

tools.name: Apache JMeter
tools.note: For apps that need heavy database or queue load (ADR-0057)

tools.name: Azure Load Testing

cost.label: Paid
cost.price: East US: $10 per resource per month, plus $0.15 per virtual user hour up to 10,000 and $0.06 after; each run bills at least 10 virtual users per engine for at least 10 minutes. A monthly virtual-user-hour limit on the resource stops tests at the cap

tools.note: Runs JMeter or Locust scripts at scale from Azure. The resource fee includes some virtual user hours; how many is not verified (ADR-0057)

cost.label: Paid
cost.price: Free for personal use only; any organization needs Business, $1,500 a year per company, or Enterprise, $2,500 a year

testKinds.name: Mutation
testKinds.checks: The tests themselves catch real bugs

authority.says: No pick: its mutation testing page walks through Stryker.NET as its example tool, without recommending it.

agent.reason: Free (Apache-2.0); the kit runs it nightly against TST-004's 85% score (ADR-0039).
